1. The Tables

This section defines the five tables, their primary and foreign keys, and the rules that the database will enforce.

data.text/markdown:
2. The Data

The data is fictional and is generated by make_data.py. The script uses random seed 42 so its results can be reproduced. The reporting date (as_of) is October 31, 2026. The data covers November 1, 2025 through October 31, 2026. The CSV files contain:
  • 25 people
  • 12 projects
  • 60 project memberships
  • 300 tasks
  • 180 expenses
Two tasks deliberately break the rule that an assignee must belong to the task's project:
  • Task 299 assigns employee 25 to project 1.
  • Task 300 assigns employee 25 to project 1.
Employee 25 exists but is not a member of project 1. Both tasks have valid employment and assignment dates. Projects 11 and 12 intentionally have no expenses. Employee 25 intentionally has no project memberships. There are also 30 unassigned tasks.

3. A Look at the Data

I read expenses.csv with Polars and counted the expense records in each month to inspect their distribution over time.

5. A Row It Refuses

I attempt to insert an expense of -50.00 for project 1. I expect the database to reject it because every expense must have an amount greater than zero.

data.text/markdown:
6. Answers You Already Knew

Before running these queries, I expect:
  1. Two employees without a manager, because the two founders report to nobody.
  2. Thirty unassigned tasks, because the data-generation script deliberately creates 30 tasks without an assignee.
  3. Zero project memberships for employee 25, because this employee was deliberately left without any project memberships.
Each query below compares its actual count with the expected count.
